title: Transactions and ACID in depth
scopeHtml: Scope: transactions, ACID mechanisms in Postgres, atomicity, constraints, durability and commit, long transactions, outbox and idempotency. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: What a transaction is
notes.html:
A transaction is a group of statements that the database treats as one unit: either all of them take effect, or none do. You open it with BEGIN, finish with COMMIT (keep everything) or ROLLBACK (throw everything away). Without BEGIN, Postgres wraps every single statement in its own tiny transaction (autocommit).

Why care? Moving money is two writes: subtract from A, add to B. If the server dies between them, money vanishes. A transaction makes the pair atomic.

Worked example. Transfer 100 from account 1 to account 2:

BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

If the second UPDATE fails (constraint, crash, deadlock), the first is undone. In Postgres, an error inside a transaction puts it in an "aborted" state: every later statement fails with current transaction is aborted until you ROLLBACK (or use a SAVEPOINT, see below).

Industry examples. Stripe-style ledgers write debit and credit rows in one transaction. Instagram-style "create post" writes the post row, the feed fan-out job row and a counter in one transaction, then publishes the job from an outbox table.

Everyday analogy. Handing cash across a counter while the cashier hands you the item: both happen or the whole sale is cancelled. Nobody walks away with both.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "a transaction is a lock". It is a unit of work; locks are one mechanism inside it.
  • Forgetting autocommit: two separate statements in a script are NOT atomic unless you wrap them.
  • Not knowing that in Postgres even DDL (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE) is transactional and can be rolled back (MySQL cannot).

notes.title: ACID overview
notes.html:
ACID is four promises: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Each one is a separate mechanism.

Letter Promise Postgres mechanism
A All or nothing MVCC row versions plus the commit log (clog / pg_xact); aborted rows are simply invisible
C Data obeys the rules Constraints, triggers, foreign keys; the app defines the rules
I Concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work MVCC snapshots plus locks (files 07 and 08)
D Committed data survives a crash Write-ahead log flushed to disk (file 09)

Decision gravity. ACID is the default you pay for. You can relax individual letters: synchronous_commit = off relaxes D for speed (a crash can lose the last ~200 ms or so of commits, but never corrupts data); lower isolation relaxes I. These are reversible config changes. Choosing a database that does not give A across multiple keys (many NoSQL stores) is a heavier, one-way architectural choice.

Everyday analogy. Sending a registered parcel: it arrives whole (A), matches the order form (C), other parcels do not get mixed in (I), and there is a signed receipt even if the van later burns down (D).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating "Consistency" in ACID as the same as "consistency" in CAP. ACID-C means "rules hold"; CAP-C means "all replicas agree" (linearizability).
  • Saying the database guarantees consistency by itself. It enforces only the rules you declared.

notes.title: Atomicity in depth
notes.html:
Atomicity means a crash or error mid-transaction leaves no trace. Postgres does not undo changes; it never overwrites a row in place. An UPDATE writes a NEW row version (tuple) and marks the old one as ended by this transaction ID (xmax). If the transaction aborts, readers consult the commit log, see "aborted", and ignore the new version. No undo log is replayed. (InnoDB differs: it changes in place and keeps an undo log.)

Each transaction gets a 32-bit transaction ID (xid) only when it first writes. Row headers store xmin (creator) and xmax (deleter). Visibility = "is xmin committed and visible to my snapshot, and is xmax not."

heap page, row for account 1
version 1: xmin=100 xmax=205  balance=500   <- ended by tx 205
version 2: xmin=205 xmax=0    balance=400   <- new
if tx 205 aborts: version 2 is ignored, version 1 is alive again

Savepoints give partial rollback inside a transaction:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders ...;
SAVEPOINT s1;
INSERT INTO order_items ...;   -- fails
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1;      -- order row kept, items undone
COMMIT;

ORMs use savepoints for "nested transactions". Each savepoint creates a subtransaction; more than 64 live subtransactions per backend overflow a cache and have caused real slowdowns on busy systems, so do not wrap every loop iteration in one.

Industry examples. Postgres's no-undo design makes rollback instant even for a huge transaction (abort is just a flag), but leaves dead rows behind for VACUUM. Oracle and InnoDB make rollback slow instead, because they must apply undo.

Everyday analogy. Writing a draft on a fresh sheet and only swapping it into the folder at the end. If you abandon it, the old sheet is still there untouched.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming Postgres uses an undo log. It uses versioned rows.
  • Forgetting that an aborted transaction still consumed space until vacuum cleans it.
  • Catching a SQL error in app code and carrying on in the same transaction without a savepoint; Postgres refuses further statements.

notes.title: Consistency and constraints
notes.html:
Consistency means every committed state satisfies the rules you declared. The database can only enforce rules it knows about, so declare them.

Constraint kinds: NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, EXCLUDE (e.g. no two overlapping bookings for a room). Constraints can be DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, checked at COMMIT instead of per statement, which is needed for circular references or swapping two unique values.

CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  balance numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)
);
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
CREATE TABLE booking (
  room int, during tstzrange,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)
);

Worked example. Two sessions both withdraw 80 from a balance of 100. With CHECK (balance >= 0) and an atomic UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE id = 1, the second blocks until the first commits, re-evaluates, sees 20, and the CHECK fails. The invariant holds with no extra code. But read-then-write in app code (SELECT then UPDATE balance = 20) can break rules that live only in app code.

Decision gravity. Put invariants in the database whenever you can: they survive every future client, script and bug. App-only validation is reversible but leaks. Adding a constraint to a big existing table needs care: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT avoids a long exclusive lock.

Everyday analogy. A form with required fields enforced by the website itself, not just by a polite note asking staff to double check.

Common interview traps.

  • Enforcing uniqueness with SELECT-then-INSERT in code (race condition); use a UNIQUE index and handle the violation.
  • Thinking foreign keys are free: they take locks on the parent row and cost writes. Still usually worth it.

notes.title: Durability and commit
notes.html:
Durability means once COMMIT returns, the data survives a power cut. Postgres achieves it by writing the change to the write-ahead log (WAL) and calling fsync before acknowledging. The heap pages themselves are flushed later (checkpoints). Details in file 09.

Settings that matter:

  • synchronous_commit = on (default): wait for WAL flush to local disk.
  • synchronous_commit = off: return before the flush; risk of losing the last few transactions (bounded by wal_writer_delay, 200 ms by default x about 3), but no corruption.
  • fsync = off: dangerous, can corrupt the whole cluster. Never in production.
  • With sync replicas: synchronous_commit = remote_apply waits until a standby has applied it.

Worked example. A cloud SSD fsync takes ~0.5 to 2 ms, so one session doing small commits sequentially tops out at roughly 500 to 2,000 commits/s. Group commit lets many sessions share one fsync, so 64 concurrent sessions can reach tens of thousands of commits/s. Batching 100 inserts per transaction cuts fsyncs 100x.

Industry examples. Stripe-style payment paths keep synchronous_commit = on with a synchronous replica. Analytics ingestion pipelines often use off for a table-heavy bulk load. Hardware matters: consumer SSDs that lie about fsync (no power-loss capacitors) break durability silently.

Everyday analogy. The receipt printed before you leave the shop. If the till computer crashes later, the paper receipt proves the sale happened.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing synchronous_commit = off can corrupt data. It can lose recent commits, not corrupt.
  • Saying COMMIT writes the table pages to disk. It writes the WAL.

notes.title: Autocommit, batching and long transactions
notes.html:
A transaction should be as short as it can be while still correct. Open a transaction, do the work, commit. Do not hold one open across a user's think time, an HTTP call or a queue wait.

Why long transactions hurt in Postgres:

  • They hold their snapshot, so VACUUM cannot remove dead rows newer than it (xmin horizon), causing bloat.
  • They hold locks, blocking others.
  • idle in transaction sessions keep all of the above while doing nothing.
-- find the offenders
SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS age, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 5;

-- guardrails (per role or database)
ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
ALTER ROLE app SET statement_timeout = '15s';

Worked example (incident pattern). A report job opens a transaction at 02:00 and sits idle in transaction for 6 hours because the app crashed mid-way holding a connection. Meanwhile 5M rows churn; VACUUM runs but cannot reclaim them; table grows from 20 GB to 35 GB and index scans slow down. Symptom: rising table size, n_dead_tup climbing, autovacuum "running" constantly. Metric: oldest xact_start age.

Batching rule of thumb. Bulk loads: 1,000 to 10,000 rows per transaction, or use COPY (often 10x or more faster than row INSERTs). Row-by-row autocommit of 1M rows means 1M fsyncs.

Everyday analogy. Keeping a library book checked out for a year "just in case". Others cannot use it and the shelf cannot be reorganised.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling a remote API inside an open DB transaction.
  • Not setting idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  • Forgetting connection poolers in transaction mode break session-level features (see file 10).

notes.title: Distributed work: outbox and idempotency
notes.html:
A database transaction cannot span "write to Postgres" and "send to Kafka". If you do both, one can succeed while the other fails. The transactional outbox fixes it: in the SAME transaction write your business row and a row into an outbox table; a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes, marking rows done. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, total) VALUES (42, 7, 99.00);
INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_id, type, payload)
VALUES (42, 'OrderCreated', '{"id":42,"total":99.00}');
COMMIT;
-- relay: SELECT ... FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL ORDER BY id
--        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100;

Idempotency key. Client sends a unique key (e.g. Idempotency-Key: pay_abc123). A UNIQUE constraint on it means a retry hits a unique violation and you return the saved result instead of charging twice.

Industry examples. Stripe documents idempotency keys for payments. Debezium reads the Postgres WAL and publishes outbox rows to Kafka (change data capture) without polling.

Decision gravity. Outbox is a safe, boring default; dual writes are a one-way bug factory. Alternatives: 2PC (heavy, file 11) or sagas (compensating steps, more app logic).

Everyday analogy. Writing "send this letter" in your own diary at the same moment you pay for the stamp; a clerk later posts every diary entry. If the clerk repeats one, the receiver ignores duplicates.

Common interview traps.

  • Dual write: save, then publish, no outbox.
  • Saying exactly-once delivery exists end to end. You get at-least-once plus idempotent consumers.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A transaction groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit; autocommit makes every lone statement its own transaction.
  • ACID: A via versioned rows plus commit status, C via declared constraints, I via MVCC and locks, D via WAL fsync.
  • Postgres has no undo log: aborted row versions are just ignored then vacuumed.
  • Put invariants in the database (CHECK, UNIQUE, FK, EXCLUDE), not only in app code.
  • synchronous_commit = off can lose recent commits but never corrupts; fsync = off can corrupt.
  • Keep transactions short; set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout; long transactions cause bloat.
  • Never dual-write to DB and broker: use the outbox plus idempotent consumers.
